summary: Alki Point Light, Seattle: an 1887 post lantern, then the 1913 octagonal tower that still flashes across Elliott Bay; a Coast Guard station automated in 1984.

lens.where: Admiralty Head Lighthouse (LighthouseFriends, HistoryLink); Salish Sea Lighthouses says the Coast Guard Museum

structures.note: Lens-lantern on a wooden post, used 1887 to 1912 (HistoryLink).
37 ft from base to lantern center (archive, LighthouseFriends). Material is disputed: archive says brick, HistoryLink says concrete and masonry.

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds and tower open during Sunday tours, May to September, 1 to 4 p.m. (Salish Sea Lighthouses); dwellings closed. LighthouseFriends reports tours canceled for high lead levels; check before going.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (Coast Guard Auxiliary also listed as owner or operator)

events.note: Lens-lantern placed atop a wooden post at the point by the Lighthouse Service.
Congress appropriated, on 28 June 1902, the $6,000 the Lighthouse Board had requested in 1895 for a fog bell and a dwelling.
Act of 17 June 1910 authorized $33,000 more, bringing the total to $47,000. The Bureau of Lighthouses received the appropriation.
Government bought the 1.5 acre tip of the point from Edmund Hanson for $9,999.
Contract awarded for the new light and fog signal after bids were rejected and readvertised (Lighthouse Service Bulletin).
Concrete fog-signal building with attached 37 ft octagonal tower. LighthouseFriends gives completion on 29 April 1913; HistoryLink gives 1 April 1913 as ready for operation.
Station activated on 1 June 1913 (LighthouseFriends).
Fourth-order Fresnel lens, made by L. Sautter and Lemonnier of Paris.
Fog signal established at Alki Point (Lighthouse Service Bulletin, 1913).
Post lantern in use since 1887 replaced by the new tower light.
Electric motor replaced one oil engine in the fog-signal building (LighthouseFriends). Commissioner list gives the light as changed to electric incandescent from incandescent oil vapor.
Commissioner asked $3,000 for improvements; the station had no workshop or storehouse, and the report called one urgent.
Lighthouse responsibilities transferred to the Coast Guard by act of 7 July 1939.
Original fog-signal equipment replaced with an electric compressor and twin horns.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced by an airway beacon.
Airway beacon flashing every five seconds; 80,000 candlepower against the lens at 13,000 (HistoryLink).
Last civilian keeper, Albert G. Anderson, retired in September 1970.
Designated as an historic place and listed on the Washington Heritage Register (HistoryLink).
Fully automated in October 1984.
Foghorn removed in August 2005.

corrections.why: The record lists the standing tower as built in 1887. The 1887 light was a lens-lantern on a wooden post; the present octagonal tower and fog-signal building were built in 1913 (archive: tower established 1913; LighthouseFriends: completed 29 April 1913).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The OpenStreetMap value of 39.0 is feet, not metres. The archive gives the light at 39 feet above mean high water, which is 11.9 m, the figure in the record.

Two different structures carry two dates. The 1887 post lantern is the first official light (archive, LighthouseFriends, HistoryLink). The 1913 tower is the present light. The record already has both.

notes_for_editor: 1) Tower material: the archive says brick; HistoryLink says concrete and masonry; the 1912 Bulletin plan says concrete. The story gives no material. 2) Completion date: LighthouseFriends gives 29 April 1913 completed and 1 June activated; HistoryLink gives 1 April 1913 ready for operation. The story gives both. 3) Denny Party and the Exact: LighthouseFriends says November 1851 (schooner Exact); HistoryLink says September 1851 (Denny Party). The story gives both. 4) First light: LighthouseFriends says Hanson 'would reportedly' light a lamp; HistoryLink calls the 1870s lantern a legend. The story says both. 5) Edmund/Edward Hanson: LighthouseFriends uses Edward and gives city directory listings 1891 to 1907; HistoryLink uses Edmund and says he kept the lamp about ten years after 1900. Roster row uses the archive span 1891-1907 as approximate. 6) Electric lighting: HistoryLink says an electric bulb replaced the lamp by 1918; the Commissioner's 1919 list gives a change to electric incandescent; LighthouseFriends dates the electric fog-signal motor to 1919. Left as stated in the story. 7) Lens location: LighthouseFriends and HistoryLink say the original Fresnel lens is at Admiralty Head Lighthouse; Salish Sea Lighthouses says the Fresnel lens was stolen in the 1970s and is now at the Coast Guard Museum. LighthouseFriends separately puts the 1887 lens-lantern at the Coast Guard Museum. Story gives both. 8) National Register: HistoryLink says in its introduction that the station is on the NRHP and later that it is eligible. No NRHP number in the record; not verified. 9) Tours: LighthouseFriends says tours were 'currently canceled' for high lead levels (page undated). Salish Sea Lighthouses gives Sunday tours May to September. The status should be checked before publication. 10) Roster name variants: LighthouseFriends has William W. Coman against the archive's William M. Coman; LighthouseFriends gives two Cameron stints (1936-1942 and 1942-1947) against the archive's one (1936-1947). 11) OCR: Bulletin 1912 p. 23 ('li ght') and 1912 p. 6 are OCR-damaged; quotes are copied as OCR'd. Check the page image. 12) Commissioner 1921 entry (cite 13) is an estimate of improvements, not a completed work; the story says the report asked for the money. 13) Commissioner 1919 entry (cite 15): the list header was not read; the story calls it a list of illuminant changes, which the entries suggest. Check the heading on the page image. 14) Newspapers: Washington newspaper searches for 'Alki Point light' gave no usable hits and 'Alki Point' with 'Hanson' returned mostly unrelated pages. No newspaper page was read. 15) The Coast Guard Auxiliary's own pages (wow.uscgaux.info) are members-only for the history page; not cited. 16) HistoryLink's essay was updated in 2007 and gives 2003 status; present-tense statements in the story come from the archive (current optic) and the Salish Sea Lighthouses page, or are marked with dates. 17) Range: HistoryLink gives 12 miles for the 1913 lens and 15 nautical miles for the 1962 beacon; the record gives 16 nm (ENC). Not used in facts. 18) Characteristic: 'Fl W 5s' from the record, matched to 'flashing once every five seconds' (HistoryLink) and 'White flash every 5 seconds' (Salish). The 1913 group-of-five pattern (LighthouseFriends) is historical. 19) Keepers' quarters: the archive gives 1887; HistoryLink and the 1913 Bulletin place the two dwellings in 1913. Story uses 1913 for the dwellings. 20) Living people: Albert G. Anderson (retired 1970) is named only as LighthouseFriends and HistoryLink name him, in his public role. Walter G. Farley (roster 1970-) is in the roster but not named in the story. The 1959-1970 Coast Guard crews appear in the roster only. 21) Other stations: New Dungeness, Patos Island and West Point carry map ids; Cape Meares, Tillamook Rock, Cape Blanco and the Columbia River lightship have no ids in the stations list. 22) Wikipedia was used only as a lead and is not cited. 18) Verification 2026-10-27: first-run quote check found all 120 quotes (none missing). Changes to the story: the 37-foot tower and the two-and-a-half-foot lens now carry metres; the first official light sentence now has its footnotes; the brick-versus-concrete disagreement is now stated in the text; 'Fog was the other hazard' is reframed to say only that the station had a fog signal (the Bulletin supports the signal, not a hazard claim); 'so about 7,000 yards' no longer implies a causal link the source does not state; the commander's move is worded as HistoryLink words it (official quarters), and the personal residence is not repeated. Checked against LighthouseFriends, HistoryLink, Salish Sea Lighthouses, the USLHS place page, the Lighthouse Service Bulletin pages 6, 15, 18, 23, 35 and 38 (1912), 2 and 26 (1913), 47 (1919), and Commissioner pages scan 439, 503, 692 (1919 to 1921). Roster lines match roster.py output; the three research-only lines (Linda Olson, Hans Martin Hanson, Edmund Hanson) carry no person slug and stay as rows.
